title: 6 cleaning businesses to start under $250
description: Six legit weekend cleaning businesses with checked starter costs, what customers pay pros, and how to land your first 3 clients.
image_alt: Infographic: 6 cleaning businesses to start under $250: pressure washing ~$195, gutter cleaning ~$140, move-out cleaning ~$150, pet waste removal ~$30, garage cleanouts ~$140, trash bin cleaning ~$230.
intro: Cleaning is one of the most reliable small businesses there is. People always need dirty things made clean, the results are easy to see, and you can start with a few tools and your weekends. You don't need a storefront, an app or a big ad budget, just good work and a way to show it.

Below are the six ideas from our post, with the starter kit we priced on real store pages, what customers typically pay professionals, and the simplest way to land your first three customers. Pick one that fits where you live and what you're comfortable doing, and get good at it before adding a second.

ideas.name: Pressure Washing
ideas.first_job: A neighbor's driveway or front walkway
ideas.what: You clean driveways, sidewalks, patios, fences and siding with a pressure washer, removing dirt, mildew and stains. Driveways and walkways are the best place to start: flat, ground-level and very visible results.
ideas.who: you like satisfying before-and-after work outdoors and are fine with getting wet.

kit.item: Briggs & Stratton 2000 PSI electric pressure washer

ideas.kit_note: The post's ~$195 total is the electric washer; most customers already have a hose and outdoor spigot you can use (ask first).

charge.text: Pressure washing prices range from **$170 to $310 on average**, with most homeowners spending **around $210**; per-area pricing runs about **$0.35 to $0.77 per square foot**.

first_customers: Wash half of your own driveway first and photograph the clean line between the two halves. That one photo sells the job.
Post it in your neighborhood Facebook group or on Nextdoor with a simple flat price for a standard driveway.
Offer to do the sidewalk of the house next door for a small add-on price while you're already set up.
ideas.watch_out: a pressure washer stream can cut skin, so never point it at people or pets, and wear closed shoes and eye protection. Start on concrete; soft wood, old siding and window seals can be damaged by high pressure. Check local rules about wash water going into storm drains.

ideas.name: Gutter Cleaning
ideas.first_job: A one-story house after the leaves have dropped
ideas.what: You scoop leaves and debris out of gutters, bag it, and check that downspouts drain. Fall and spring are the busy seasons, and many homeowners want it done every year.
ideas.who: you're comfortable and careful on a ladder and want a seasonal service with repeat customers.

kit.item: Work gloves and a gutter scoop

ideas.kit_note: The post's ~$140 total is the ladder plus gloves and a plastic gutter scoop. A 6 ft ladder suits one-story homes only.

charge.text: The average U.S. homeowner spends **$167 on gutter cleaning**, and most cleanings cost **between $119 and $234**, or about **$0.95 to $1.25 per linear foot**.

first_customers: Clean your own or a family member's gutters and take photos of the full scoop of muck next to the clean gutter.
Walk single-story neighborhoods with lots of trees and leave a flyer with a flat one-story price.
Offer a spring return visit at a small discount so every fall customer becomes a repeat customer.
ideas.watch_out: stick to one-story homes, set the ladder on firm, level ground, never stand on the top step, and have someone with you. Stay well away from power lines, and don't work on wet or icy days.

ideas.name: Move-Out Cleaning
ideas.first_job: A friend's apartment before they hand back the keys
ideas.what: You deep-clean empty homes and apartments so tenants get their deposit back or sellers can hand over a clean house: kitchens, bathrooms, inside cabinets, floors, baseboards and windowsills.
ideas.who: you're thorough, don't mind scrubbing, and want work that comes in steadily around the end of every month.

kit.item: Sponges, microfiber cloths and all-purpose spray
kit.amazon: cleaning sponges microfiber cloths all purpose cleaner

ideas.kit_note: The post's ~$150 total is the shop vac plus sponges and an all-purpose spray. Add supplies as jobs come in.

charge.text: Move-out cleaning costs **$0.15 to $0.25 per square foot**, or **$150 to $500 total** on average, typically **$25 to $50 per hour, per person**.

first_customers: Write a clear move-out checklist (inside oven, fridge, cabinets, baseboards) and share it with every quote. Landlords love checklists.
Introduce yourself to small local landlords and property managers; they need empty units cleaned between tenants.
Post in local moving, college and apartment groups near the end of each month, when leases end.
ideas.watch_out: never mix cleaning products (especially bleach with ammonia or acids), keep windows open and wear gloves. Agree in writing on what's included and do a walk-through with the client before and after.

ideas.name: Pet Waste Removal
ideas.first_job: A neighbor's backyard with one dog
ideas.what: You visit yards on a regular schedule (usually weekly) and scoop, bag and dispose of dog waste. It's the cheapest idea on the list to start, and customers tend to stay on a weekly plan for a long time.
ideas.who: you're not squeamish, like being outside, and want simple, recurring weekly income.
ideas.kit_note: The post's ~$30 total is the scooper plus a box of sturdy bags.

charge.text: Dog waste removal costs about **$15 to $30 per week** for one dog, **$20 to $40 per visit** every other week, and **$60 to $150** for a one-time cleanup.

first_customers: Offer a one-time "spring/fall yard reset" to a few neighbors with dogs, then invite them onto a weekly plan.
Ask local dog walkers, groomers and pet sitters if you can leave a card; they hear about busy owners first.
Group customers on the same few streets so each route takes less driving.
ideas.watch_out: wear gloves, wash your hands well, and disinfect your scooper and shoes between yards so you don't spread germs or parasites from one yard to the next. Close every gate behind you and check where your town allows pet waste to be disposed of.

ideas.name: Garage Cleanouts
ideas.first_job: A family member's cluttered one-car garage
ideas.what: You help customers sort what to keep, donate and toss, then sweep and vacuum the garage and put things back neatly. You're selling a weekend of hard work they don't want to do.
ideas.who: you're organized, can lift and carry, and enjoy turning a mess into an orderly space.

kit.item: Heavy-duty contractor trash bags and work gloves

ideas.kit_note: The post's ~$140 total is the shop vac plus heavy trash bags and gloves. If you also do Move-Out Cleaning, it's the same shop vac.

charge.text: Professional garage cleanouts average **$150 to $500 for a 1-car garage** and **$250 to $800 for a 2-car garage**.

first_customers: Do a free or discounted cleanout for a friend or relative in exchange for before/after photos and a review.
Post the transformation in local groups in spring and fall, when people tackle garages.
Partner with real estate agents: sellers often need garages cleared before listing photos.
ideas.watch_out: lift with your legs and get help with heavy items. Old paint, chemicals, batteries and propane tanks can't go in regular trash, so check your town's hazardous waste drop-off rules. Agree up front who hauls items away; large haul-aways may need a truck or a junk service.

ideas.name: Trash Bin Cleaning
ideas.first_job: Your own and your neighbors' bins on pickup day
ideas.what: You wash, degrease and deodorize customers' curbside trash and recycling bins right after pickup day, when they're empty. Most customers sign up for a monthly or quarterly cleaning.
ideas.who: you want a simple route-based service and don't mind smelly work. If you already own a pressure washer for Idea 01, your starting cost drops a lot.

kit.item: Briggs & Stratton 2000 PSI electric pressure washer
Degreaser and a stiff scrub brush

ideas.kit_note: The post's ~$230 total is the pressure washer plus degreaser and a stiff brush.
first_customers: Clean your own bins and your next-door neighbors' for free on pickup day, and take before/after photos of the inside.
Leave a door hanger on every house on your street with your price and the day you'll come by (the day after pickup).
Offer a small discount when three or more neighbors on one street sign up, so your route is quick.
ideas.watch_out: dirty bin water shouldn't go into storm drains, so check your city's rules on where wash water can go before you start. Wear gloves and eye protection, and ask permission before using a customer's outdoor spigot.

getting_started: **Check local rules.** Search "[your city] business license" to see whether you need one. Rules vary by city and state, and some places also regulate where wash water can drain.
**Think about insurance.** Ask a local agent about general liability insurance before ladder, pressure washing or in-home work; one accident can cost more than a season's income.
**Set clear prices.** Write a simple price list (per driveway, per story, per visit) and give written quotes by text so there are no surprises.
**Take payment simply.** Use a payment app you already have and send a receipt for every job.
**Track every dollar.** Keep receipts for tools and supplies; side income is taxable, so set some aside.
tip: Send a **before and after photo** with every quote. It does the selling for you.

faq.q: Which of these is cheapest to start?
faq.a: Pet waste removal, at about $30 for a pan-and-rake scooper and sturdy bags. Gutter cleaning and garage cleanouts are next at about $140 each.

faq.q: Do I need a business license?
faq.a: It depends on your city and state. Many places require a general business license for paid services, even part-time. Search your city's website or call the clerk's office before you start.

We don't promise earnings. The ranges above are what customers typically pay professionals, from published cost guides. As a beginner, expect to charge less until you have reviews and photos of your work.

faq.q: Can I combine a few of these?
faq.a: Yes. Pressure washing and trash bin cleaning share the same washer, and move-out cleaning and garage cleanouts share the same shop vac, so adding a second service costs little.
Pet waste removal and trash bin cleaning are good starter jobs for teens with a parent's OK. Skip ladder work and pressure washers until you're older, and check your state's rules for working minors.
